evidence.says: The author of Divining Science is Warren Alexander Dym, who received a history PhD from UC Davis in 2005 and was at the University of Miami.
Warren Alexander Dym's dissertation Divining Science: Treasure Hunting and the Saxon Mining Industry, 1500-1800 was completed at UC Davis in 2005.
Warren Dym was a visiting assistant professor at Bucknell and a 2009–10 research fellow.

basis: The book author and dissertation author are linked by the UC Davis degree, and a Warren Dym was at Bucknell around the review date. The sources found do not establish that the Bucknell reviewer and the book or dissertation author are the same person.

evidence.says: Steven Bucklin's faculty page lists Realism and American Foreign Policy, The Wilsonian Legacy in Political Science, and a 1993 University of Iowa PhD in history.
The University of Iowa history newsletter lists Steven Bucklin's The Wilsonian Legacy in Political Science among its 1993 dissertations.

basis: The University of South Dakota faculty page attributes works from both keys to Steven Bucklin and identifies his 1993 Iowa history doctorate. Iowa's history newsletter independently lists the dissertation under his name.

evidence.says: Robert Ellis of Regent’s Park College, Oxford, authored What I Have Learned From Baptist History; the article gives ORCID 0009-0009-6390-4457.
They Need Nothing (2012) is by Robert Richmond Ellis, Norman Bridge Distinguished Professor of Spanish at Occidental College.
Rob Ellis reports appointments at Regent’s Park College from 2001, as principal from 2007 until retirement in 2021.

basis: The 2026 article identifies its author with the ORCID on b and Regent’s Park College. His account of his career at Oxford overlaps with the 2012 book author’s professorship at Occidental College, establishing two different careers.

evidence.says: American Expansionism (2003) is by Mark S. Joy, then associate professor at Jamestown College.
Cites Mark Stephen Joy's Into the Wilderness as a 1992 PhD dissertation at Kansas State University.

basis: The sources identify the book author and the dissertation author, but do not establish that they are the same person. Their compatible names and subjects alone are insufficient for a merge.

evidence.says: The author of The Irish in New Orleans describes attending Tulane for a Ph.D. in history.
Laura D. Kelley's Erin's Enterprise is listed as a Tulane University Ph.D. thesis from 2004.
The publisher names Laura D. Kelley as author of The Irish in New Orleans and describes her moving to New Orleans to complete her Ph.D.

basis: The book's author describes attending Tulane for her history Ph.D.; the library association identifies the thesis as Laura D. Kelley's 2004 Tulane doctorate. The matching degree and institution support one career, although the sources do not explicitly connect the two titles.

evidence.says: Athletes in academe is credited to Patrick Bryant Miller, born 1951; They cried to the Lord is credited to Patrick D. Miller, born 1935.
Patrick D. Miller Jr. (1935–2020) earned a Harvard PhD and taught at Princeton Theological Seminary from 1984 to 2005.

basis: The records identify the author of the sports dissertation as Patrick Bryant Miller, born in 1951, and the author of the biblical study as Patrick D. Miller, born in 1935. Their different birth years establish two people.

evidence.says: The article cites Herman A. Norton as author of both Struggling for Recognition and the Vanderbilt dissertation on Confederate military chaplaincy.
The catalogue attributes Struggling for Recognition to Herman Albert Norton and dates it 1977.

basis: A scholarly article cites the book and dissertation under the same author, Herman A. Norton. The book catalogue identifies that author as Herman Albert Norton, linking the works on both keys.

evidence.says: Christine Schultz White wrote Opothleyahola, factionalism, and Creek politics, a 1986 TCU history dissertation.
Christine Schultz White held a TCU PhD and was on the Alabama School of Mathematics and Science faculty in 1996.
Christine White, author of British and American Commercial Relations with Soviet Russia, received a Cambridge PhD in 1988.
Christine White of Pennsylvania State University presented a paper on the US and the Far Eastern Republic in 1991.

basis: The book author and the TCU dissertation author have different doctorates and careers, supporting different people. Key b appears mixed: its dissertation belongs to Christine Schultz White, while its Penn State affiliation and supervision may belong to the Soviet historian on key a; review those claims separately before any identity action.

evidence.says: Editor Alan Hayes is a researcher at National University of Ireland, Galway and publisher of Arlen House.
Crossref metadata credits the Tobin review to Alan L. Hayes, ORCID 0000-0001-9158-0255, Wycliffe College, University of Toronto.
Alan L. Hayes earned a BA in 1967 and a PhD in 1975 and joined Wycliffe College in 1975.
Arlen House publisher Alan Hayes describes studying at Galway, working in its library and relaunching Arlen House in 1999.

basis: The review is tied by its ORCID and affiliation to the Wycliffe historian, whose degree and teaching career began decades before the Galway publisher's career. The publisher identifies the editor of the other key's book as the Arlen House publisher; the two careers are distinct.

evidence.says: Kathleen Cairns of the History Department, Cal Poly San Luis Obispo, reviewed The Fairer Death for H-Law in July 2007.
Kathleen A. Cairns, author of The Enigma Woman and Front-Page Women Journalists, is a history lecturer at Cal Poly San Luis Obispo.
Cal Poly's history department lists Kathleen Cairns and her books Front-Page Women Journalists and Proof of Guilt.

basis: The 2007 review credits Kathleen Cairns at Cal Poly San Luis Obispo. The catalogue identifies the author of books on the other key as a history lecturer at the same institution, and the department lists those books under Kathleen Cairns.
